sec.title: Background
sec.p: ABBV-368 is a humanized monoclonal antibody that targets the costimulatory receptor OX40. Here, we investigate a treatment strategy with ABBV-368 combined with the investigational toll-like receptor 9 agonist tilsotolimod, the programmed cell death 1 inhibitor budigalimab, and nab-paclitaxel in patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (R/M HNSCC). To our knowledge, this is the first clinical study in this setting to investigate chemotherapy combined with three immunotherapy agents, aiming to overcome failure of prior immune checkpoint inhibition and chemotherapy.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This phase 1b, multicenter, open-label study (NCT04196283) enrolled adult patients with R/M HNSCC into one of three treatment arms: ABBV-368 with tilsotolimod, ABBV-368 with tilsotolimod and nab-paclitaxel, or ABBV-368 with tilsotolimod, nab-paclitaxel, and budigalimab. Patients were treated in 28-day cycles. ABBV-368, nab-paclitaxel, and budigalimab were administered intravenously and tilsotolimod via intratumoral injection. Study objectives included safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and preliminary antitumor activity. In addition, biomarker analyses were performed.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Overall, 30 patients were enrolled; 16 received ABBV-368 plus tilsotolimod, 7 ABBV-368 plus tilsotolimod and nab-paclitaxel, and 7 ABBV-368 plus tilsotolimod, nab-paclitaxel, and budigalimab. In total, 80% of patients experienced any-grade adverse events related to ABBV-368. ABBV-368 and tilsotolimod induced peripheral interferon-gamma pathway upregulation, Th1 cytokine production, and T-cell activation that was not negatively impacted by nab-paclitaxel. There were no responses in the ABBV-368 plus tilsotolimod arm; one partial response was demonstrated in both the ABBV-368 plus tilsotolimod and nab-paclitaxel, and ABBV-368 plus tilsotolimod, nab-paclitaxel, and budigalimab arms, corresponding to an overall response rate of 14.3%.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The quadruple combination of ABBV-368, tilsotolimod, nab-paclitaxel, and budigalimab was well tolerated and demonstrated pharmacodynamic activity. Several patients had disease stabilization, but clinical responses were limited. Initial priming and T-cell immune activation were inadequate to overcome prior therapy resistance mechanisms including a hypothesized unfavorable tumor microenvironment. Future work investigating strategies to target this inhibitory tumor microenvironment with optimally scheduled immunotherapy combinations in selected patients and indications is urgently needed to improve patient outcomes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Head and neck cancers have a high mortality rate, with over 430,000 deaths annually. Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) accounts for >90% of cases.1 Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapies, specifically anti-programmed cell death protien-1 (PD-1) agents, have been approved for treatment of patients with HNSCC in the frontline setting alone or with chemotherapy based on results from the KEYNOTE-048 study.2 3 However, many patients do not respond to therapy, and those who do often develop resistance, with few subsequent therapy options available for patients with recurrent/metastatic (R/M) HNSCC.1 A retrospective cohort study in patients treated with immunotherapy for R/M HNSCC between the years 2015 through 2023 found a median survival of only 10.9 months from the start of ICI-containing therapy, highlighting a clear need for improved therapies.4

Three key elements that contribute to failure of initiating or maintaining an antitumor response to ICI therapy are (1) insufficient dendritic cell (DC) activation and CD8+T cell cross-presentation; (2) insufficient tumor infiltration and amplification of CD8+T cell proliferation; and (3) rapid tumor growth that denies immunotherapy the time needed to establish antitumor control.5 In preclinical models, the first two elements were addressed by combining anti-PD-1 agents, OX40 agonists, and toll-like receptor (TLR) 9 ligands, resulting in control of tumor lesions receiving intratumoral therapy and distant tumors.6 7 Clinically, the humanized recombinant monoclonal antibody ABBV-368 is an OX40 agonist that has shown a favorable safety profile and evidence of antitumor activity in solid tumors.8

To help overcome anti-PD-1 resistance and improve clinical responses in HNSCC, we sought a treatment combination strategy to target different steps of the immune response. The synthetic TLR9 agonist tilsotolimod was included to address insufficient antigen priming, while the use of ABBV-368 was hypothesized to enhance the longevity of T-cell activation both intratumorally and in the periphery. The cytotoxicity agent nab-paclitaxel was chosen to address fast tumor growth since it is a well-established salvage chemotherapy that can be administered with lower-dose or no steroid premedication, which could impair immune responses induced by immunotherapy.9 Finally, to sustain the activated immune response, budigalimab was included to combat induced upregulation of PD-1 and its ligand (PD-L1), and T-cell exhaustion.

In this study, we investigated the clinical hypothesis that intratumorally delivered TLR9 agonist, in combination with ABBV-368 and nab-paclitaxel and supported by anti-PD-1 therapy, can trigger a T-cell immune response to overcome ICI resistance in patients with second-line-and-beyond HNSCC for whom chemotherapy and prior immunotherapy have failed.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This phase 1b, multicenter, open-label study (NCT04196283) investigated three combination therapies (figure 1) in adult (≥18 years) patients with histologically or cytologically confirmed HNSCC that previously progressed during or after three or fewer prior treatment regimens administered in the R/M setting. Required among prior treatments, unless considered ineligible, were platinum-based therapy (either in the definitive or advanced R/M setting) and an immunotherapy regimen that included a PD-(L)1 inhibitor.

caption.title: Study design and treatment. For all treatment arms, the cycle length was 28 days. aThe C1D2 dose of ABBV-368 (striped box) was removed during a protocol amendment. This dose was received by three patients prior to the amendment. C, cycle; D, day.

sec.p: ABBV-368 was combined with tilsotolimod (arm 1), tilsotolimod and nab-paclitaxel (arm 2), or tilsotolimod, nab-paclitaxel, and budigalimab (arm 3). The primary objective was to assess safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics; the secondary objective was to assess preliminary antitumor activity per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) V.1.1. Exploratory objectives included preliminary antitumor activity per immune RECIST and pharmacodynamic and predictive biomarkers analyses. Detailed information on treatment, eligibility criteria, and analyses is in online supplemental methods.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: 30 patients were enrolled in the study (ABBV-368+tilsotolimod arm, n=16; ABBV-368+tilsotolimod/nab-paclitaxel arm, n=7; ABBV-368+tilsotolimod/nab-paclitaxel/budigalimab arm, n=7; online supplemental table S1). Median patient age was 56 years (range 29–76); most patients were male (77%), had baseline Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 1 (80%), and had metastatic disease at study entry (60%). Nine patients (30%) had received ≥4 prior lines of systemic therapy.

sec.title: Drug exposure
sec.p: Median exposure to ABBV-368 across all patients was 69 (range 13–237) days, with patients receiving a median of four doses (range 1–10; online supplemental table S2). Median exposure to ABBV-368 was longest in the ABBV-368+tilsotolimod/nab-paclitaxel/budigalimab arm (median 97 days; range 27–237) and shortest in the ABBV-368+tilsotolimod arm (median 53.5 days; range 13–181). Median exposure to tilsotolimod had a similar pattern to ABBV-368. Median exposure to nab-paclitaxel was 56 (range 14–57) days and was comparable between arms that included this agent. Median exposure to budigalimab was 56 (range 28–198) days. At the time of analysis, all patients had discontinued ABBV-368 and budigalimab, and six (43%) had discontinued nab-paclitaxel. The most common reason for discontinuation for each drug was progressive disease (PD; online supplemental table S3).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: All patients who received ABBV-368 experienced treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), which included PD for this study. The most frequent TEAEs overall were fever (43%), nausea (40%), constipation (37%), and asthenia (37%). Grade ≥3 TEAEs occurred in 23 patients (77%); the most common were malignant neoplasm progression (30%), anemia (17%), and pneumonia (13%). Any-grade treatment-related AEs (TRAEs; per investigator) related to ABBV-368 occurred in 80% of patients; the most common were vomiting (13%), constipation, diarrhea, asthenia, fatigue, fever, and hypothyroidism (10% each; online supplemental table S4). The three cases of fever were grade 1–2 (n=1 in each treatment arm). One patient in the ABBV-368+tilsotolimod/nab-paclitaxel/budigalimab arm experienced increased alanine and aspartate aminotransferases related to ABBV-368 (both grade 1). One case of cytokine release syndrome (grade 1) related to ABBV-368 was observed in the ABBV-368+tilsotolimod arm. Grade ≥3 ABBV-368 TRAEs were reported by three patients (10%), all in arm 1: one patient experienced hepatitis and dermatitis bullous requiring steroids; one patient experienced angioedema, dyspnea, and pneumonitis requiring steroids and malignant neoplasm progression; one patient experienced chest pain and injection site pain not requiring steroids.

Serious ABBV-368-related AEs occurred in four patients (13%; online supplemental table S5). TEAEs led to ABBV-368 discontinuation in nine patients (30%); three events were considered related to ABBV-368 (fatigue, septic shock, malignant neoplasm progression; n=1 each).

15 deaths occurred during the study, all with primary cause being PD. Among 10 patients (33%) with a TEAE leading to death, only 1 was assessed as possibly treatment-related (malignant neoplasm progression deemed related to both ABBV-368 and tilsotolimod).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Efficacy outcomes are presented in figure 2, and online supplemental figure S2 with potential clinical covariates such as lines of prior therapy and PD-L1 status. There were no responses in the ABBV-368+tilsotolimod arm; median progression-free survival (PFS) in this arm was 1.6 months (95% CI 1.0 to 2.3). In the ABBV-368+tilsotolimod/nab-paclitaxel arm, the overall response rate (ORR) was 14.3% (1/7 patients) and median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI 0.5 to non-estimable). The one patient with a response in this arm (partial response (PR)) had received two prior treatment regimens (cisplatin; nivolumab) and had a duration of response of 3.5 months. In the ABBV-368+tilsotolimod/nab-paclitaxel/budigalimab arm, the ORR was 14.3% (1/7 patients) and median PFS was 1.8 months (95% Cl 1.0 to 3.5). The one patient in this arm with a response (PR) had three prior treatment regimens (nivolumab; 5-fluorouracil+carboplatin+cetuximab; cetuximab) and a duration of response of 5.6 months.

sec.title: Biomarkers
sec.p: Peripheral blood samples collected on cycle (C)1 day (D)2 after tilsotolimod treatment but prior to ABBV-368 administration showed transcriptional upregulation of the interferon (IFN)-γ pathway signature, as well as increased levels of IFN-γ and its downstream chemokine, CXCL10 (figure 3). ABBV-368 treatment induced upregulation of MOXI, a surrogate biomarker for OX40 engagement (data not shown), on CD4+central memory (CM) T cells (CD28+CD95+; online supplemental figure S1A). MOXI upregulation was sustained across treatment arms, suggesting that tilsotolimod and nab-paclitaxel did not negatively impact OX40 activation. Consistent with T-cell activation, PD-1 was upregulated on CD4+CM T cells in all treatment arms (figure 3D). The upregulation was detected early (C1D2, post-tilsotolimod) and was sustained at high levels prior to budigalimab administration on C3D1 in arm 3. Patients with a PR had higher peripheral T-cell activation, assessed by CD25 upregulation on CD8+T cells, than patients without response (online supplemental figure S1B). Patients with a baseline biopsy PD-L1 combined positive score ≥1% tended to have longer PFS across all arms (p=0.0096, HR 0.15, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.63), though numbers in this analysis were limited (online supplemental figure S2).

sec.title: Case study
sec.p: A female patient in her 40s diagnosed with metastatic human papillomavirus-negative HNSCC (primary tumor site in the oral cavity) entered the study after three prior lines of therapy, including cisplatin and nivolumab. She was treated with ABBV-368 plus tilsotolimod and nab-paclitaxel (arm 2) and experienced tumor size reduction (figure 4A).

caption.title: Case study results. (A) CT scans made before and after treatment. The arrow points to the tumor. (B) Fold change in CD4+effector memory T cells (CD45RA−CD62L−) in patients with clinical benefit (SD+PR). (C) ctDNA response from baseline. (D) Target lesion percentage change from baseline. (E) Mutation analysis over time. C, cycle; CB, clinical benefit; CNV, copy number variation; ctDNA, circulating tumor DNA; D, day; FV, final visit; PD, progressive disease; PR, partial response; SD, stable disease.

sec.p: Significant T-cell expansion was seen post-treatment in peripheral blood, as evidenced by a 150-fold increase by C1D15 in CD4+effector memory T cells (CD45RA−CD62L−; figure 4B). Changes in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA; median mutant molecules/mL of plasma (mMTM)) were examined from baseline through final visit (FV). mMTM increased by 36.6% from baseline to C1D15, then declined to −89.7% from baseline at C3D15, remaining below baseline levels through FV (figure 4C). These changes coincided with a reduction in the sum of diameters of the tumor target lesions, particularly at C3D15 (−40%; figure 4D).

Mutations in GNA11, PDGFRB, PIK3CA, and TP53 were detected at baseline; however, by C3D15, these mutations were undetectable (figure 4E). Similarly, MET gene amplification was detected at baseline, became undetectable by C1D15, and remained undetectable through FV. Together, these results suggest a clearance of certain tumor mutations with treatment that coincided with clinical benefit. Pathogenic PIK3CA (His1047Arg) and TP53 (Tyr107*) mutations were detected again at FV, along with a notable gain-of-function missense alteration in AKT (Glu79Lys) that had not been present at baseline. The eventual tumor lesion progression coincided with the rising ctDNA fraction at FV. The re-emergence of the PIK3CA His1047Arg mutation and acquisition of AKT Glu79Lys, together with the published association between PI3K/AKT pathway activation and inferior clinical response to immunotherapy,10 implicate the re-activation of PI3K/AKT signaling as a potential mechanism of resistance in this patient.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Combinations of OX40 agonists and ICIs have been investigated in multiple relapsed/refractory solid tumors with limited success.11 In this study, encouraging signals of on-target biological activity were observed in nearly all patients in arm 1 (ABBV-368+tilsotolimod). Early in the course of treatment, the combination of ABBV-368 and tilsotolimod led to immune cell activation and upregulation of the IFN-γ pathway as expected.12 In fact, a rapid local inflammatory response was observed in the first two patients treated with the original study design, requiring a protocol modification to stagger ABBV-368 and tilsotolimod administration to improve tolerability. With this adjustment, ABBV-368 and tilsotolimod combinations were generally well tolerated; symptoms consistent with low-grade cytokine release syndrome and immune-related AEs including low-grade fevers and pneumonitis were observed but did not lead to substantial study discontinuations. Immune cell activation did not translate into frequent clinical responses, however.

Many factors could be underlying the paucity of clinical activity in these heavily pretreated patients. Draining lymph nodes are essential for T-cell priming and an abscopal effect, and their ablation in HNSCC from prior therapies could severely reduce immunotherapy efficacy due to a loss of conventional DCs and decreased circulating T cells.13 Better efficacy for this combination might be observed in the neoadjuvant setting, prior to lymph node irradiation, as was seen in patients with resectable, locally advanced HNSCC when neoadjuvant pembrolizumab was added to standard of care, resulting in significantly improved event-free survival.14 Additionally, the hypothesis that an abscopal effect could be achieved in patients with HNSCC by injecting a single lesion with tilsotolimod was supported by a prior study in melanoma.15 However, HNSCC tumors display substantial intrapatient heterogeneity and are generally less inflamed and responsive to immunotherapy than melanoma;16 therefore, injecting multiple lesions may have improved efficacy.16

Pharmacologic variation in intratumoral tilsotolimod administration may have also contributed to reduced efficacy.17 18 The protocol treatment regimen requiring multiple sequential intratumoral injections was complex, raising questions around its utility in a real-world setting. Overcoming and optimizing intratumoral injection challenges18 and/or developing tolerable and effective systemic TLR agonist administration options would improve feasibility and has been investigated in many studies.1921

An important aspect of any T-cell agonist therapy is the impact of dose and schedule on immunomodulatory pharmacology, safety, and efficacy.22 The complete saturation of checkpoint receptors or ligands by therapeutic antibodies may not be optimal for conventional bivalent OX40 agonists that aim to induce the trimeric engagement required for optimal downstream signaling. The dose and schedule for ABBV-368 used in this study was established in a first-in-human study.8 Next-generation OX40 agonists, such as the hexavalent OX40 agonist INBRX-106, are being investigated with the goal of enhancing receptor clustering, independent of Fc-mediated crosslinking, to boost antitumor T-cell responses.11 23 24 Adding to the challenge of targeting OX40, recent work revealed that less than 20% of patients with cancer have high OX40 and low OX40L expression patterns that might be amenable to OX40 agonist enhancement.25

Low response rates may also have resulted from an excessively immunologically suppressive tumor microenvironment. Tertiary lymphoid structures in the tumor microenvironment have been shown to correlate with enhanced response to immunotherapy in HNSCC.13 In this study, only one such structure was identified in 1 of 17 samples (data not shown). Another local cellular mechanism that may impair responses to ICI is inhibitory regulatory T cells.2628 OX40 is expressed on both antitumor T-effector cells and immunosuppressive CD4+regulatory T cells (Tregs). One proposed mechanism of action of OX40 agonists is impairment of the suppressive function of Tregs; however, recent data contradict this hypothesis.29 Preclinical studies support targeting and immunological depletion of inhibitory Tregs, which are abundant in HNSCC30 and have been identified as a major player in immunotherapy failure.2728 3133 A study specifically targeting the additional axis of CCR8+Tregs in combination with budigalimab in patients with HNSCC is ongoing (NCT05005403).

The third arm of this study sought to capitalize on the preclinical therapeutic benefit of combining T-cell agonists targeting costimulatory receptors and ICI.34 The combination approach taken in this study is novel in that it separates the OX40 agonist and anti-PD-1 therapy due to the preclinical concern for co-administration antagonism.35 36 Unfortunately, only four of the seven patients in arm 3 stayed on study long enough to receive budigalimab infusion (C3D1). The early display of T-cell exhaustion (PD-1 expression on CD4+CM T cells seen on C2D15) may have blunted the immune response, and earlier administration of budigalimab could have potentially rescued this. Furthermore, sustained IFN signaling has indeed been linked to checkpoint resistance in non-small cell lung cancer and melanoma.37 38

Beyond the effects of the immune therapy, it is also possible that the clinical responses observed were driven by chemotherapy rather than the immune agonists. However, peripheral blood pharmacodynamic biomarkers and clinical responses generally being restricted to injected tumors support an immune mechanism. In total, these clinical data did not support further investigation of the combination of tilsotolimod and ABBV-368, and none of these arms will be tested further.

In summary, we investigated a treatment strategy aimed at overcoming resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy and PD-1 inhibition in R/M HNSCC through a rational combination of chemotherapy, immune agonists, and ICI targeting different stages of the immune cycle. While all treatment combinations were tolerated, the success of our approach was limited. We posit that initial priming and T-cell immune activation were inadequate to overcome an unfavorable tumor microenvironment, possibly due to the presence of immunosuppressive Tregs and delayed sequencing of budigalimab. Future work that takes these factors into consideration for more-optimal combination strategies is urgently needed to improve outcomes for patients with HNSCC.

Data availability free text: AbbVie is committed to responsible data sharing regarding the clinical trials we sponsor. This includes access to anonymized, individual, and trial-level data (analysis data sets), as well as other information (eg, protocols, clinical study reports, synopses, or statistical analysis plans), as long as the trials are not part of an ongoing or planned regulatory submission. These clinical trial data can be requested by any qualified researchers who engage in rigorous, independent, scientific research, and will be provided following review and approval of a research proposal, Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP), and execution of a Data Use Agreement (DUA). Data requests can be submitted at any time after approval in the USA and Europe and after acceptance of this manuscript for publication. The data will be accessible for 12 months, with possible extensions considered.
